PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 50 — Lesson 74: Endocrine & Metabolic Assessment

FNP-level goal: Assess hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, diabetes complications, thyroid symptoms, adrenal concerns, unexplained weight change, and metabolic risk using physiology, a focused history and examination, appropriate laboratory interpretation, safe disposition, and closed-loop follow-up. Recognize diabetic ketoacidosis/hyperosmolar crisis, severe hypoglycemia, thyroid storm/myxedema concern, adrenal crisis, and endocrine presentations that cannot safely remain in routine outpatient care.

Learning Objectives

  • Use a physiologic framework for symptoms of glucose, thyroid, cortisol, electrolyte, and volume disturbance.
  • Distinguish screening, diagnosis, monitoring, and acute triage; a lab value does not mean the same thing in each setting.
  • Interpret A1C, plasma glucose, TSH/free T4, electrolytes, and cortisol-related testing in clinical context and recognize important limitations.
  • Identify diabetes, thyroid, and adrenal red flags requiring emergency evaluation or expedited specialty input.
  • Assess common endocrine complications involving cardiovascular, renal, neurologic, eye, foot, reproductive, and mental-health systems.
  • Create a patient-centered plan with medication reconciliation, result ownership, access-aware follow-up, and explicit safety-net instructions.

Part 1 — Start With Stability, Not the Diagnosis Label

Endocrine symptoms may evolve slowly, but endocrine emergencies can deteriorate rapidly. Begin with vital signs, mental status, hydration/perfusion, respiratory effort, ability to take fluids/medications, vomiting, abdominal pain, focal neurologic symptoms, infection/stressor history, and medication access. Ask whether the patient uses insulin or other glucose-lowering medication, corticosteroids, thyroid medication, diuretics, or drugs that can affect glucose or electrolytes.

Emergency patterns include altered mental status, syncope/seizure, severe or recurrent hypoglycemia, marked dehydration, persistent vomiting, deep/labored breathing, suspected ketoacidosis/hyperosmolar crisis, shock, severe electrolyte abnormality, acute adrenal-crisis symptoms, fever/tachyarrhythmia/agitation with severe thyrotoxic features, or hypothermia/bradycardia/hypoventilation with severe hypothyroid features. Do not let a familiar chronic disease—such as diabetes or hypothyroidism—create false reassurance when physiology is unstable.

Part 2 — Build an Endocrine Problem Representation

Translate the complaint into a concise physiologic statement. For example: “A patient with diabetes and several days of vomiting, polyuria, tachycardia, dehydration, and confusion” is not simply “high glucose”; it is an acute volume, metabolic, and possible acid-base emergency. “A patient with weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, palpitations, and new atrial fibrillation” suggests excess thyroid-hormone effect until evaluated. “Weakness, nausea, hypotension, and hyperkalemia after abrupt glucocorticoid interruption” raises concern for adrenal insufficiency.

Document timing, trajectory, precipitating infection/illness/surgery/stress, pregnancy possibility when relevant, prior endocrine diagnosis, family history, autoimmune history, recent weight change, dietary pattern, supplements, alcohol/substances, sleep, mood, and social barriers. A medication list is part of the endocrine examination: missed insulin, access problems, incorrect administration, steroids, antipsychotics, diuretics, thyroid products, supplements containing thyroid hormone, and biotin-related laboratory interference can change the differential.

Part 3 — Diabetes Assessment: Mechanism Explains the Symptoms

Hyperglycemia can cause polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, fatigue, blurred vision, recurrent infection, unintentional weight loss, and dehydration. Excess filtered glucose produces osmotic diuresis; water and electrolytes follow, so tachycardia, orthostasis, dry mucosa, weakness, and kidney injury can develop. Symptoms alone do not establish diabetes type or severity, and a home glucose meter is useful for self-monitoring but does not by itself establish a new diagnosis.

Ask about onset, glucose trend, ketone testing when relevant, insulin use and delivery technique, missed doses, food access, sick-day plan, recent infection, new medications, steroid exposure, pregnancy, nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain, breathing pattern, mental status, urinary symptoms, foot wounds, vision change, chest pain, and neurologic symptoms. Do not assume a person with type 2 diabetes cannot develop ketosis, or that a person who looks comfortable is not becoming dehydrated.

Part 4 — Screening, Diagnosis, and Monitoring Are Different Questions

Laboratory tests for diabetes include A1C, fasting plasma glucose, random plasma glucose in the appropriate symptomatic setting, and oral glucose tolerance testing. A1C reflects an approximate three-month average glucose exposure, whereas plasma glucose is a point-in-time measure. In an asymptomatic patient, an abnormal diagnostic result generally requires confirmation using an appropriate second measurement; acute classic symptoms or a hyperglycemic crisis changes the urgency and interpretation.

Ask whether the test fits the patient. A1C can be misleading when red-cell lifespan or hemoglobin behavior is altered, including some anemias, transfusion, hemoglobin variants, kidney disease/dialysis, or recent blood loss. If the A1C and glucose pattern disagree, do not automatically choose the number that fits expectations; investigate the discrepancy and use an appropriate alternate measure or diagnostic pathway.

Part 5 — Hyperglycemic Emergencies: Think Volume, Ketones, and Osmolality

DKA is characterized by insulin deficiency with ketosis and metabolic acidosis; hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is characterized by profound hyperglycemia, dehydration, and hyperosmolality, often with marked mental-status change. Either can be precipitated by infection, interruption of therapy, new diabetes, myocardial ischemia, stroke, medications, or another stressor. They are not safely diagnosed or treated through a single outpatient glucose value.

Concerning features include persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, inability to tolerate oral intake, deep or labored breathing, fruity breath, progressive dehydration, tachycardia, hypotension, weakness, confusion, lethargy, or a high glucose pattern with ketones. Obtain emergency evaluation when clinical concern exists. In acute care, diagnostic workup commonly addresses glucose, electrolytes, renal function, acid-base status, ketones, osmolality, precipitating cause, and cardiac/infectious context; the exact protocol belongs to the treating setting.

Part 6 — Hypoglycemia: Identify the Immediate Threat and the Cause

Hypoglycemia can present with sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, confusion, behavior change, weakness, seizure, loss of consciousness, or an atypical presentation in older adults or people with impaired awareness. The immediate question is whether the patient can safely self-treat and protect their airway. Severe symptoms, inability to take oral carbohydrate, recurrent lows, seizure, altered consciousness, or unsafe living circumstances require emergency action rather than routine medication adjustment by message.

After the immediate episode is addressed, find the mechanism: excessive insulin/secretagogue exposure, missed meals, vomiting, increased activity, alcohol, kidney/liver dysfunction, weight change, drug interactions, impaired counterregulation, or dosing/administration error. Ask the patient to show, not merely describe, their devices and usual workflow when feasible. “Nonadherence” may instead be affordability, confusing instructions, food insecurity, low health literacy, or a device problem.

Part 7 — Diabetes Complications: Every Visit Is a Systems Assessment

Diabetes assessment includes cardiovascular symptoms/risk, blood pressure, kidney status, albuminuria as appropriate, neuropathic symptoms, foot skin integrity, pulses, sensation when indicated, vision change/retinal-care status, infections, dental/oral health, sexual function, depression, and medication safety. A normal A1C does not erase hypoglycemia, comorbidity, or barriers to care; conversely, a high A1C should prompt a reasoned review rather than blame.

New focal neurologic deficit, chest pain, acute vision loss, infected/ischemic foot, rapidly spreading cellulitis, severe kidney injury, or signs of sepsis have their own urgent pathways. Avoid teaching patients that a “diabetes follow-up” can wait when they have symptoms suggesting stroke, acute coronary syndrome, limb-threatening infection, or another emergency.

Part 8 — Thyroid Assessment: Symptoms Are Clues, Not a Diagnosis

Thyroid hormone affects energy use, heart rate, temperature regulation, bowel function, skin/hair, mood, menstrual/reproductive function, and neuromuscular activity. Hypothyroid symptoms may include fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, weight gain, bradycardia, and slowed cognition. Hyperthyroid symptoms may include heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, palpitations, anxiety, increased stool frequency, and atrial arrhythmia. These patterns overlap with anemia, depression/anxiety, medication effects, infection, menopause, cardiopulmonary disease, malnutrition, and malignancy.

TSH is often the initial test, interpreted with free T4 and, in selected situations, T3 and thyroid antibodies. A high TSH often supports primary hypothyroidism, while low TSH often supports hyperthyroidism, but pituitary disease, severe illness, pregnancy, medications, and assay interference can complicate interpretation. If TSH is abnormal, additional testing is generally needed to define the cause. Do not diagnose or dose-adjust from symptoms alone without considering adherence, timing, interactions, and the full laboratory context.

Part 9 — Thyroid Red Flags and Nodule Safety

Urgently assess a patient with severe thyrotoxic features such as fever, marked tachycardia/arrhythmia, agitation/delirium, heart failure, severe diarrhea/vomiting, or a precipitating illness. Also escalate severe hypothyroid concern when there is hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, altered mental status, or profound functional decline. These are not routine laboratory-follow-up situations.

For a thyroid nodule or neck mass, ask about duration, growth, neck pressure, dysphagia, dyspnea, voice change, radiation exposure, and family history. Rapidly enlarging neck swelling, stridor, significant compression symptoms, or airway concern requires urgent evaluation. Imaging and biopsy decisions should follow a risk-based pathway; palpation cannot reliably characterize all nodules.

Part 10 — Adrenal Assessment: Cortisol Supports Stress Physiology

Cortisol supports vascular tone, glucose availability, and the response to physiologic stress. Adrenal insufficiency can present with fatigue, weight loss, nausea/vomiting, abdominal symptoms, weakness, orthostasis/hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia in primary disease, and hypoglycemia. Ask specifically about known adrenal disease, pituitary disease, chronic steroid exposure, recent steroid taper/cessation, autoimmune history, infection, anticoagulation/bleeding risk when relevant, and severe illness or surgery.

Adrenal crisis can cause severe pain, vomiting/diarrhea, weakness, confusion, loss of consciousness, hypotension/shock, low glucose, low sodium, and high potassium. It requires immediate emergency treatment. Do not delay emergency disposition while seeking confirmatory outpatient cortisol testing in an unstable patient with a compatible history. Stable diagnostic workup and long-term glucocorticoid management require current specialist-informed protocols.

Part 11 — Weight Change, Fatigue, and the Broad Differential

Unexplained weight loss or gain, fatigue, and temperature intolerance should not automatically become a thyroid test order only. Integrate nutrition/food access, depression/anxiety, sleep apnea, medication/substance effects, pregnancy/postpartum context, diabetes, heart/kidney/liver disease, inflammatory disease, infection, gastrointestinal disease, malignancy, and social stress. Use the review of systems and examination to generate a prioritized differential.

Targeted testing should follow the problem representation. Broad untargeted endocrine panels can create incidental abnormalities and false certainty. A safe FNP plan specifies what diagnosis each test is evaluating, how results will be reviewed, and what symptom change requires urgent care before results return.

Part 12 — Focused Examination and Diagnostic Planning

The examination may include weight trend, orthostatic vital signs when appropriate, hydration, mental status, skin/hair changes, tremor, thyroid/neck, heart rhythm, lungs, abdomen, edema, neurologic function, feet, pulses, sensation, injection sites, and signs of infection. Examination findings refine probability; they do not replace glucose, electrolyte, renal, acid-base, thyroid, or endocrine testing when physiology is in question.

Build diagnostic plans by asking: What is the immediate danger? What is the likely mechanism? What result changes disposition? What limitations apply to this test? Who owns follow-up? This prevents the common error of ordering an A1C, TSH, or cortisol-related test without a plan for discordant results, worsening symptoms, or referral access.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: Vomiting and High Glucose

A 23-year-old with diabetes has missed insulin during a viral illness and now has polyuria, vomiting, abdominal pain, tachycardia, dry mucosa, and deep rapid breathing.

FNP reasoning: this is not a routine refill visit. The pattern raises concern for DKA and significant dehydration. Arrange immediate emergency evaluation for metabolic and precipitating-cause assessment.

Part 14 — Clinical Case: Palpitations and Weight Loss

A 62-year-old reports tremor, heat intolerance, unintentional weight loss, palpitations, and a newly irregular rapid pulse.

FNP reasoning: hyperthyroidism is a key consideration, but the irregular tachyarrhythmia may be immediately important. Assess hemodynamic stability, obtain the appropriate cardiac pathway, and use thyroid testing to define rather than merely name the disorder.

Part 15 — Clinical Case: Steroid Interruption and Shock

A patient on chronic glucocorticoids stopped medication abruptly during gastroenteritis and presents with vomiting, weakness, confusion, low blood pressure, low glucose, and high potassium.

FNP reasoning: adrenal crisis is a life-threatening consideration. Emergency treatment/disposition comes before outpatient confirmation or routine medication counseling.

FNP Endocrine & Metabolic Assessment Framework

  1. Assess stability first: mental status, airway/breathing, perfusion, glucose, hydration, vomiting, infection, electrolyte/acid-base concern, and medication access.
  2. Translate symptoms into physiology: insulin deficiency/resistance, counterregulation, thyroid excess/deficiency, cortisol deficiency/excess, volume and electrolyte effects.
  3. Separate testing goals: screening, diagnosis, monitoring, acute triage, and complication surveillance are different clinical questions.
  4. Interpret in context: verify timing, assay limits, red-cell/hemoglobin effects on A1C, severe illness, medications, pregnancy, and discordant results.
  5. Screen systems, not just numbers: cardiovascular, renal, neurologic, eye, foot, reproductive, mental-health, and social risks.
  6. Escalate red flags: DKA/HHS concern, severe hypoglycemia, adrenal crisis, thyroid storm/myxedema features, sepsis, stroke/ACS signs, and limb-threatening infection.
  7. Close the loop: result owner, treatment/referral access, medication reconciliation, and explicit emergency precautions.

High-Yield Summary

Diabetes: polyuria/polydipsia can reflect osmotic diuresis; assess dehydration, ketones, medication access, and acute triggers.
A1C: estimates recent average glycemia but can be misleading when red-cell or hemoglobin factors alter interpretation.
DKA/HHS concern: vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, altered breathing/mental status, ketones, or severe hyperglycemia need emergency assessment.
Hypoglycemia: protect the airway and assess severity first; then identify dosing, food, organ function, alcohol, activity, access, and device factors.
Thyroid: symptoms guide the differential; TSH plus free T4 and context help define the disorder.
Adrenal crisis: hypotension, vomiting/diarrhea, weakness, confusion, glucose/electrolyte abnormalities, and steroid/adrenal history are an emergency pattern.
FNP standard: integrate physiology, diagnostics, medication safety, equity/access, disposition, and closed-loop follow-up—not a single lab result.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Endocrine testing, glucose management, insulin or steroid decisions, imaging, referral, emergency disposition, and follow-up must follow current evidence, local protocols, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
